 Why Asian Paints Lost Its Moat
 By HDFC SKY | Published at: Oct 23, 2026 11:56 AM IST
 Asian Paints built one of India’s strongest consumer-business advantages. But weak demand, falling market share, and aggressive new competition have challenged its long-standing dominance.

 Introduction 
 For years, Asian Paints was considered one of the safest stories in India’s consumer sector. Its brand was familiar, its distribution network was difficult to replicate, and its relationships with dealers and painters gave it an advantage that went well beyond advertising.
 The company had built a business where competitors could manufacture paint, but matching its distribution, product range, and market presence was far more difficult. This was the moat investors often referred to when explaining why Asian Paints commanded a premium valuation .
 That confidence began to weaken after 2021, and the pressure became much more visible in 2024 and 2025. Demand slowed, competition intensified, and Aditya Birla Group’s Birla Opus entered the market with substantial manufacturing capacity and aggressive pricing.
 Asian Paints did not suddenly become a weak business. It remained the market leader, but the factors that had protected its position for decades began facing a serious test.
 How Asian Paints Built Its Moat 
 The paint business looks relatively simple from the outside. A customer chooses a colour, buys the paint, and gets the walls painted. Behind that transaction, however, is a complex network involving manufacturers, dealers, contractors, painters, and consumers.
 Asian Paints spent decades building relationships across this network.
 Its advantage was not based only on brand recognition. The company developed a wide product portfolio, an extensive distribution system and a strong understanding of local consumer preferences. It also invested in technology and supply-chain capabilities that helped dealers manage inventory and customers select products.
 For dealers, stocking a brand involves more than buying cans of paint. They want products that sell consistently, reliable supply, attractive margins, and support from the manufacturer. For consumers, the brand reduces uncertainty around quality, colour, and finish. Painters and contractors influence the final purchase as well.
 Asian Paints became deeply embedded in this ecosystem. This created a cycle that supported its growth. A strong brand attracted customers, customer demand encouraged dealers to stock the products, and the extensive dealer network made the brand easier to access. The scale of the business also supported advertising, product development, and distribution investments.
 This was the moat. The question was whether it could withstand a competitor willing to spend heavily to build an alternative network.
 Why The Paint Market Is Attractive 
 India’s paint industry has traditionally offered long-term growth potential because painting demand is linked to housing, renovation, urbanisation, and rising household incomes.
 The decorative paints segment is particularly important. It includes products used in homes, offices, and other buildings, ranging from economy paints to premium finishes. Unlike some industrial businesses, decorative paints have a direct connection with household consumption. Customers may repaint a home during a renovation, before a festival, after moving into a new property, or simply when they want to change the appearance of a space.
 The market also has room for premiumisation. Consumers who previously selected basic products may gradually move towards better finishes, waterproofing solutions, specialised textures, and premium colours.
 Asian Paints built a strong position in this market over several decades. Its challenge was that the opportunity was attractive enough to draw competitors with significant financial resources.
 The Entry of Birla Opus Changed the Competition 
 The competitive environment changed substantially when the Aditya Birla Group entered the paints industry through Birla Opus.
 Birla Opus launched in February 2024, backed by a large investment programme and plans to establish manufacturing facilities across India. The entry was different from that of a small regional competitor because the group had the financial capacity to invest in plants, distribution, and marketing at scale.
 The company also used aggressive pricing and dealer incentives to attract channel partners.
 According to Elara Securities data reported by Reuters in May 2025, Asian Paints’ market share fell from 59% to 52% in the 12 months ending March 31, while Birla Opus reached a market share of 6.8% in the latest quarter. These figures refer to estimates reported during the early phase of Birla Opus’ expansion, rather than an independently verified current market-share position.
 The speed of the change surprised several market observers. Asian Paints had spent decades building its position, while Birla Opus gained visibility within a relatively short period.
 That does not mean the new entrant had already replicated the entire Asian Paints business. Market share, dealer relationships, profitability, and customer loyalty are different measures. However, the early numbers showed that competitors could make meaningful progress when they entered with sufficient capital and a clear expansion strategy.
 Why Dealer Relationships Matter So Much 
 A paint company’s relationship with its dealers is one of the most important parts of the business.
 Consumers may recognise a brand, but the dealer often influences which products are available, how they are priced, and what alternatives are offered. Painters and contractors can also influence the final decision, especially when customers are unsure about product quality or application.
 Asian Paints had built a strong dealer network over many years. This network was one of the reasons its business was difficult to challenge.
 However, a moat based partly on distribution can come under pressure when a new competitor offers attractive commercial terms. Dealers may be willing to give shelf space to a new brand if the margins are appealing, demand appears promising, or the manufacturer offers strong support.
 Reports on Birla Opus’ entry highlighted deep discounts, dealer incentives, and efforts to recruit experienced employees from established paint companies. Reuters also reported that Birla Opus was setting up factories close to Asian Paints’ existing manufacturing locations.
 The competitive battle was, therefore, not limited to television advertising or product quality. It extended to the distribution system that had historically protected Asian Paints.
 The Demand Slowdown Made Things Worse 
 Competition would have been challenging under normal market conditions. It became more difficult because the paint industry was already experiencing weak demand.
 In FY2024-25, Asian Paints reported that subdued consumer sentiment and muted demand had affected the domestic decorative paints business. In the fourth quarter, domestic decorative revenue declined 5.2%, while volume growth was 1.8%.
 This difference between volume and revenue is important. A company can sell more product but still report lower revenue if the product mix changes, prices decline, or customers shift towards lower-priced offerings.
 Asian Paints’ management described the year as challenging, citing weak demand and increased competitive intensity. The combination meant that paint companies were competing for a smaller or slower-growing pool of demand while also trying to protect their market share.
 When demand is strong, companies may be able to grow without taking business directly from competitors. In a slow market, winning new customers often means taking share from another brand.
 That is what made the timing of Birla Opus’ entry particularly disruptive.

 Why Asian Paints’ Margins Came Under Pressure 
 Asian Paints had historically benefited from strong operating margins. Its scale, brand strength, distribution network, and product mix helped it generate attractive profitability.
 But margins can weaken when a company faces pressure on both revenue and costs.
 Paint manufacturers use several raw materials derived from petrochemicals and other industrial inputs. Changes in crude oil prices, solvents, chemicals, and packaging costs can affect production expenses. The impact depends on the company’s ability to manage costs and pass price increases on to customers.
 At the same time, competitive pressure can restrict pricing flexibility. If a rival is offering discounts or lower prices, an established company may find it difficult to increase prices without risking volume or market share.
 Asian Paints’ FY2025 results reflected this pressure. Consolidated net profit fell approximately 33% to ₹3,667.2 crore, while PBDIT margin declined to 17.8%, a reduction of 360 basis points, according to The Economic Times.
 The company also acknowledged that it would need to spend more on branding, distribution, and market activity to respond to the competition.
 This creates a difficult trade-off. Spending more may help protect market share, but it can also reduce margins in the short term. Cutting expenditure may protect profitability but could allow competitors to gain more visibility and dealer support.
 The Stock Market Started Questioning the Premium 
 Asian Paints was not valued like an ordinary paint manufacturer.
 For years, investors were willing to pay a premium because they believed the company’s business advantages would support steady growth and strong returns over time. The valuation reflected expectations around brand strength, distribution, profitability, and the company’s ability to defend its market position.
 That premium became harder to justify when growth slowed and competition increased.
 The stock had reached its 2021 highs during a period when investors were willing to pay high valuations for companies with strong brands and predictable earnings. However, the performance weakened in the following years.
 The Indian Express reported that Asian Paints’ stock had fallen around 35% from its September 2021 highs by January 2025, even though the company had recorded strong profit growth during the preceding three financial years.
 In November 2024, the stock also experienced a sharp decline after the company reported a 42% fall in quarterly net profit. Asian Paints shares closed at ₹2,542.65, their lowest closing level since April 2021, according to The Economic Times.
 The market was not merely reacting to one weak quarter. Investors were reassessing whether Asian Paints could maintain its earlier combination of market share, pricing power, and high profitability.
 Has Asian Paints Actually Lost Its Moat? 
 The answer depends on how a moat is defined.
 If a moat means that no competitor can enter the market or take market share, then Asian Paints never had such protection. Paint manufacturing is not an industry where entry is impossible.
 But if a moat means a combination of brand recognition, distribution reach, product knowledge, dealer relationships, and operational scale, Asian Paints still possesses substantial advantages.
 The company continues to have a large manufacturing network, an established brand, and significant reach across the Indian market. Its annual report describes the business as India’s leading paint and décor company, with installed decorative paint manufacturing capacity of 2.29 million kilolitres per year in India.
 The more relevant question is whether these advantages can continue generating the same level of returns as they did in the past.
 A moat can remain intact while becoming less profitable. A company may still lead the market but have to spend more on discounts, advertising, and distribution to defend that position. In that case, the moat has not disappeared, but its economic value may have changed.
 This is the concern investors have been debating around Asian Paints.
 The Threat Is Bigger Than Birla Opus 
 Birla Opus has received most of the attention, but Asian Paints is facing pressure from several directions.
 Existing competitors such as Berger Paints, Kansai Nerolac, and Akzo Nobel India continue to operate in the market. JSW Paints has also expanded its presence, while regional players remain relevant in different parts of the country.
 The industry is moving towards a more competitive structure. New entrants can invest in manufacturing, while established players can use their existing distribution networks and product portfolios to defend their positions.
 The result may be a market where companies have to work harder to maintain their share and profitability.
 Asian Paints’ management has said that the company is responding through distribution expansion, retail partnerships, product innovation, and differentiated offerings. In FY2025, the company reported that it was present across more than 169,000 retail touchpoints and had increased its supplier count.
 However, building a stronger defence will require investment. The company cannot assume that its historical brand strength alone will be enough.
 Asian Paints Is Also Expanding Beyond Paint 
 Another part of the company’s strategy is its move into home décor and related categories.
 Asian Paints has expanded into areas such as lighting, furnishings, décor products, and painting services. Its Beautiful Homes platform is intended to help the company participate in a larger portion of the home-improvement journey.
 The logic is understandable. If a consumer is already using Asian Paints to renovate a home, the company may have an opportunity to sell other products and services connected with that project.
 But diversification brings its own challenges.
 Home décor categories can have different customer preferences, competitive structures, and profitability profiles compared with paints. The company must, therefore, build capabilities in new categories without allowing investments to distract from its core business.
 Asian Paints’ FY2025 disclosures indicated that its home décor business experienced a muted performance, while the company also recognised an impairment related to its investment in White Teak.
 The expansion could create new revenue opportunities over time, but it is not an immediate substitute for protecting the company’s core paint business.
 What Asian Paints Needs to Defend 
 The company’s response will likely involve several elements rather than one major decision.
 It needs to protect its dealer relationships, maintain product availability, and remain competitive across different price segments. It also has to manage its brand spending carefully because aggressive discounts may help volumes but can affect profitability.
 Product innovation will be another factor. Premium paints, waterproofing solutions, specialised finishes, and other differentiated products can help companies move away from pure price competition.
 Asian Paints has continued to invest in product development and reported the launch of several new products in FY2025. Its management also highlighted innovation and differentiated product offerings as part of its response to changing market conditions.
 The company’s scale remains an advantage, but scale becomes less valuable if competitors can use capital to match manufacturing capacity and offer attractive terms to dealers.
 Asian Paints, therefore, has to prove that its brand and distribution network can generate superior returns even in a more competitive market.
 What Happens to the Stock from Here? 
 The stock’s future performance will depend on how the market assesses the company’s earnings and competitive position.
 A recovery in demand could help the entire industry, but it may not automatically restore Asian Paints’ earlier margins. The company would also need to demonstrate that it can defend market share without excessive discounts or marketing expenditure.
 On the other hand, if competition remains aggressive, investors may continue to assign a lower valuation to the business than they did during its strongest growth years.
 The distinction between business quality and stock valuation is important. Asian Paints can remain a leading paint company while its stock delivers weaker returns if earnings growth does not meet the expectations built into its valuation.
 Similarly, a period of margin pressure does not necessarily mean the company’s long-term competitive advantages have disappeared.
 The market will be watching revenue growth, volume trends, market share, margins, dealer relationships, and the performance of new business segments.
 The next phase of the story will depend on whether Asian Paints can use its brand and distribution advantages to defend its position without sacrificing the financial performance that once made it one of India’s most admired consumer businesses.

 Why is Asian Paints losing market share?
 Asian Paints has faced increased competition from Birla Opus and other paint companies, along with weak demand in the decorative paints market. Reports in 2025 indicated a decline in its market share during the first year of Birla Opus’ expansion.
 What is the moat of Asian Paints?
 Asian Paints’ moat has traditionally included its brand strength, extensive distribution network, dealer relationships, product portfolio, manufacturing scale, and understanding of the Indian consumer market.
 Is Birla Opus a threat to Asian Paints?
 Birla Opus is a significant new competitor because it has entered the market with substantial financial backing, manufacturing investments, and aggressive dealer and pricing strategies. Its long-term impact will depend on whether it can maintain market share and build a profitable distribution network.
 Why did Asian Paints’ profit decline in FY2025?
 Asian Paints faced weak demand, increased competition, adverse product mix, and pressure on operating margins. Consolidated profit declined approximately 33% in FY2025, according to reported financial results.
 Has Asian Paints lost its market leadership?
 Asian Paints remained the leading company in India’s decorative paints market, although reported market share estimates showed a decline during 2024–25. Market leadership and competitive strength are not the same as maintaining the same market share or margins.
 Why is Asian Paints’ stock under pressure?
 The stock has faced concerns around slower growth, declining market share, increased competition, margin pressure, and the possibility that the company may need to spend more to defend its position.
 Can Asian Paints regain its market share?
 Asian Paints has several established advantages, including its brand, distribution network, and manufacturing scale. Whether it regains market share will depend on demand conditions, competitive pricing, dealer relationships, product innovation, and the effectiveness of its response to new entrants.
